key_insight: LLMs that show fewer measured cognitive biases are not automatically better decision makers — some biases can be functional and improve outcomes in specific contexts.
problem_solved: Challenges the assumption that reducing measurable cognitive biases always improves LLM decision quality, by identifying a mismatch between bias metrics and real-world decision performance.
method: Benchmark a range of cognitive biases in multiple LLMs using behavioral decision-making tasks and structured prompts.
Measure decision quality/outcomes for the same tasks and correlate bias scores with performance across different contexts.
Analyze when and why certain biases are adaptive (helpful) versus harmful, including controlled prompt/intervention checks.
impact: Encourages practitioners to evaluate models by task-aligned decision outcomes rather than treating all bias as error; informs more nuanced mitigation strategies that preserve contextually useful heuristics.
visual_elements: Scatter plot of "bias score" vs "decision quality" showing weak or context-dependent correlations
Heatmap or matrix showing contexts/tasks where specific biases improve vs degrade outcomes
Flowchart of the experimental pipeline: prompts → bias assessment → outcome measurement → correlation analysis
Icon-based vignette contrasting "debiasing" (crossed-out bias icon) versus "context-aware calibration" (balance scale)
paper_title: LLMs displaying less cognitive bias are not necessarily better decision makers
paper_authors: Vittoria Dentella, Marco Marelli, Luca Rinaldi
